output.framing:
The proposal is a small experiment rather than a settled optimization: cache the Jira transition reads a single selection makes, then judge from what the cache changes whether the repeats cost enough to justify the extra state. That fits the project's "no optimization without evidence" principle, provided the experiment can produce evidence either way — today it is an open question, not a claimed win.

One factual nuance worth keeping in view, as the design stands: in the idea-selection path the captured issue's transitions are read twice for different reasons — before the claim, to find the move into the active status, and after the claim, to snapshot the transitions publication later relies on. Those are answers about two different statuses, and the claim write is what changes the answer, so a cache must either be invalidated by that write or risk serving the pre-move answer where the design wants the post-move one. If "repeated reads" means something else — per-candidate probes, retries, or several selections in one process — say so and the picture changes. My reading is open to correction; no refinement change has been made yet.
questions: Which reads are in scope: the pre-claim lookup and the post-claim snapshot within one selection, per-candidate eligibility probes, or repeats across a retry or several selections in one run?

What would count as the reads mattering — added latency in the selection step, request count against Jira's limits, or visible delay to the operator — and would counting and timing the reads be acceptable evidence before any cache exists?

If a cache is kept, which principle governs it: "one selection works from a single transition snapshot" or "never ask Jira the same question twice"? The two differ exactly at the claim move, where the design currently wants a fresh answer — and the choice also decides where the cached state lives: in the Jira adapter, shared by every caller, or inside the selection action.

output.contribution: Worth pursuing as an experiment, with one premise worth checking before any cache is designed. In the selection code today the two transition reads of one idea are not repeats of the same question: the pre-claim lookup finds the move out of the submitted status, the claim write changes the answer, and the second read is the snapshot publication is designed to consume instead of re-reading Jira later (select-idea/index.ts:157, 190, 195; publish-decision/index.ts:227, 469). A cache invalidated by the claim write therefore saves nothing on that path, and a cache that survives it serves a stale answer where the design wants the fresh one. The same-question repeats, if any, are the ones the author should name: per-candidate probes for ineligible items, a retry or recovery attempt of a retained selection, or something else. Counting and timing requests first is cheap and can settle the question either way.
output.fit: This belongs to the project's enduring direction rather than to a current design choice. The clearest surviving statements of direction are evidence-driven and experiment-first: AGENTS.md:16 requires evidence of a bottleneck before performance complexity, and the idea-refinement spec (docs/idea-refinement/spec.md:20, 51) says an exploratory idea needs no trial plan while exploring a performance idea before measurement is explicitly allowed. Existing capabilities make the probe cheap: the Jira adapter is built over an injectable transport (src/adapters/jira.ts:217-219), the test helper already records every operation call (tests/support/jira.ts:33-60), and the idea selection already retains the transitions it observed (select-idea/artifacts.ts:34-45), so request counts and timing can be captured without new run-time state. The snapshot-at-claim read pattern is a current choice, not purpose: if measurement showed the reads matter, revisiting when publication's transitions are captured would be a legitimate later question. "The reads do not justify a cache" is a successful result here.
steering: Keep the null result first-class: say that a measured absence of material repeats ends the exploration, since exploration without a pay-off is acceptable at this stage.

Before state, count: attribute the Jira requests of one selection to distinct questions and attempts, using the injectable transport or a recording wrapper, so the experiment produces evidence even if no cache is ever added.

If the author's repeats are the pre-claim lookup and the post-claim snapshot, keep the claim write in view as the invalidation point; if they mean per-candidate probes, retries, or several selections in one run, name it, because only those can be answered by a cache.

If a cache is kept, the choice of where the cached state lives is a real trade-off worth stating, not settling: the adapter performs requested operations while the action owns the claim decision, so the invalidation knowledge sits with the action.
constraints: Adapter/action boundary: adapters perform explicitly requested operations and actions own eligibility, claiming and desired statuses (docs/adapters/architecture.md Responsibility; docs/adapters/jira.md Interface). The event that makes a transitions read stale is the claim write, which the adapter does not own, so shared cache state needs an invalidation signal it cannot observe.

Deliberate freshness: selection re-reads source state before claiming to preserve intervening human changes (docs/task-engine/actions/select-task.md:52, 59). A cache that survives selection attempts weakens that property, and persisting one across process restarts adds staleness risk.

Full-cost rule (AGENTS.md): cache state brings invalidation rules, failure handling, tests and documentation obligations; nothing in the current documents, code or history records Jira rate-limit pressure or measured selection latency, so the justification has to come from the experiment.
evidence: No README, purpose, charter or vision document exists in the current tree; docs/ holds design documents only, and the former README and docs/LONG_TERM_VISION.md were removed in commit 8935d55 ("Remove legacy implementation and retain Nexus rebuild design").

Removed but still direction-bearing history: docs/LONG_TERM_VISION.md in 8935d55^ - "Evidence-driven. An interesting idea is not an improvement. Prefer hypotheses, experiments, baselines, and measurable outcomes", "Experiment Before Infrastructure ... seek the cheapest evidence that could change the decision", and the decision test "Should we validate the hypothesis before implementing it?"; the removed README stated Nexus's purpose as "useful, verified engineering work with minimal human coordination".

src/task-engine/actions/select-idea/index.ts:156-168 reads transitions to find the move into the active status; :190 applies that move; :195 reads transitions again to snapshot those available from the active status.

src/task-engine/actions/publish-decision/index.ts:226-235 and :469 use only the captured snapshot (selection.transitions.fromActive); src/task-engine/actions/select-idea/artifacts.ts:34-45 documents the same intent; docs/adapters/jira.md:57-60 - "the run uses that snapshot for all agent work and publication. It does not re-read the issue, comments or available transitions later in the run."

src/task-engine/actions/select-task/index.ts:143-152 reads transitions once per fresh claim; workflows/finite-delivery.ts:10-20 loops selection for the next task, so repeated selections in one run address different issues; workflows/idea-refinement.ts:19-39 selects one idea per run.

src/adapters/jira.ts:366-372 performs one HTTP request per readTransitions with no cache, retry or rate-limit handling; src/adapters/jira.ts:217-219 takes the transport as a parameter and tests/support/jira.ts:33-60 records operation calls, so request counting needs no cache.

AGENTS.md:16 "Avoid premature optimization: Require evidence of a bottleneck before adding performance complexity"; docs/idea-refinement/spec.md:20 "An exploratory idea does not need a benchmark or trial plan merely to be worth pursuing"; :51 "avoiding premature optimization does not prohibit exploring a performance idea before measurement".
uncertainty: The one-sentence description does not say which reads are in scope; my reading (the pre-claim lookup and post-claim snapshot of one idea selection) may differ from the author's meaning (per-candidate probes, retries, or repeat selections).

No measurement exists yet: whether any repeated read is material for latency or request count is exactly what the experiment would show, and neither docs nor code record Jira limits or observed selection latency.

Direction is inferred: the clearest purpose and vision statements were removed from the tree in 8935d55 and survive only in history, so the fit argument rests on AGENTS.md principles and current architecture documents.

output.contribution: Three discoveries reshape this experiment. First, on the claim path the two transitions reads inside one fresh idea selection are answers about two different statuses — the pre-claim read is asked while the issue is still in Submitted, the post-claim read is asked after the write moved it into the active status, and that post-claim snapshot is exactly what publication later consumes instead of re-reading (the run is documented never to re-read the issue, comments or available transitions). A cache keyed on the question — issue, caller, status, query parameters — therefore gets no hit inside one selection; the reuse this idea can chase lives in retries, repeated attempts or repeated selections in one process, and measuring which of those actually repeat is what the experiment can settle. Second, Jira documents read-composition alternatives that remove reads with no cached state at all: `expand=transitions` on the existing issue read (and on JQL search), a bulk fetch with the transitions expand, and a bulk available-transitions read covering up to 1,000 issues per call. Third, “the reads mattering” has several currencies — selection wall-clock, hourly points, per-endpoint burst headroom, operator-visible delay or failed selections — and Atlassian’s own guidance is to cache stable responses with ETags and conditional headers, while AWS’s caching guidance decides caches by measured hit ratio and downstream call counts. Nothing here argues against the experiment; it shows which readings would make the answer legible whichever way it turns out.
findings: Project evidence (current read shape): on the fresh-claim path the idea selection calls the transitions endpoint twice — `transitionInto`/`selectFresh` read an issue’s permitted transitions to find the move into the active status, then `claim` reads them again right after the status write and stores the result as `transitions.fromActive` (src/task-engine/actions/select-idea/index.ts, around lines 155-201). The finite-delivery selection reads transitions once (src/task-engine/actions/select-task/index.ts, claim). So a retained or resumed selection that skips the pre-claim read does one read, not two.

Project evidence (why the second read exists): [publish-decision](src/task-engine/actions/publish-decision/index.ts) consumes the saved post-claim snapshot (`selection.transitions.fromActive`) rather than reading transitions again, and [docs/adapters/jira.md](docs/adapters/jira.md) states the run uses the selection snapshot for all agent work and publication and does not re-read the issue, comments or available transitions later. One of the two reads is already the design’s chosen substitute for a later read, so removing it changes a design promise rather than only a request count.

Project evidence (the two reads are different questions): Jira answers about the status in force when the read happens, and the claim write is what changes that status. Because the answer also depends on the caller’s permissions and workflow conditions, a status-aware cache cannot hit inside one fresh selection, and a cache that ignored status would serve the pre-move answer where the design wants the post-move one. This matches the editor’s reading; the experiment can confirm the scope empirically (per-candidate probes, retries, several selections per process).

Project evidence (current documented stance on caches): [docs/tech-stack.md](docs/tech-stack.md) says «Cache only deterministic validation results with their inputs declared. Live service operations and completion checks are never replaced by cached validation results.» A transitions read is a live provider observation rather than a validation result, so this idea sits beside that rule rather than clearly under it; as intent, that sentence is itself a current choice an idea may revise.

Project evidence (contracts bearing on where state would live): [docs/adapters/architecture.md](docs/adapters/architecture.md) says adapters «Return observed results», and AGENTS.md says to keep specialized guarantees within the component or action that needs them, with components depending on provider-owned public contracts. An adapter-level cache would need the adapter to own the invalidation guarantee, or “observed” quietly becomes “remembered”; an action-level cache keeps the staleness decision inside the selection it serves.

Project evidence (what the code can observe today): the transport the adapter accepts returns only `{status, body}` (src/adapters/jira.ts, JiraHttpResponse), so no timings and no response headers are visible to callers, and any non-2xx response — including 429 — becomes a fault with no retry loop. Counting and timing the reads therefore needs its own observation point, and today a rate-limit event surfaces as a failed selection rather than as a retry.

Project evidence (existing timing trail): activity-log entries are written with a receipt timestamp per activity packet (src/application/activity-log.ts) and the operator interface timestamps each entry once on receipt ([docs/operator-interface.md](docs/operator-interface.md)). The wall-clock span of a selection step is therefore partly recoverable from today’s logs, while individual Jira requests are not separately recorded.

Jira fact (transitions endpoint semantics): GET /rest/api/3/issue/{issueIdOrKey}/transitions «Returns either all transitions or a transition that can be performed by the user on an issue, based on the issue’s status»; a request for a transition that does not exist or cannot be performed returns an empty transitions list; the list is empty when the user lacks the Transition issues permission; the answer accepts `transitionId`, `includeUnavailableTransitions` (default false), `skipRemoteOnlyCondition` and `sortByOpsBarAndStatus`, and can be expanded with `transitions.fields` (Jira Cloud REST API v3, Issues; accessed 2026-09-27). The permission clause is why the same question can have different answers for different callers.

Jira fact (the same answer can be folded into other reads): GET /rest/api/3/issue/{issueIdOrKey} accepts `expand=transitions` («Returns all possible transitions for the issue»), and the Issue response schema carries a `transitions` array described as «The transitions that can be performed on the issue»; POST /rest/api/3/search/jql also accepts a transitions expand (accessed 2026-09-27). Whether the expanded list is identical to the dedicated endpoint’s answer — availability filtering, ordering, `isAvailable` flags — is something the experiment can compare directly for one issue and status.

Jira fact (bulk alternatives): POST /rest/api/3/issue/bulkfetch accepts a transitions expand but then caps at 100 issues per request (1,000 requires omitting it), and GET /rest/api/3/bulk/issues/transition returns available transitions for up to 1,000 issues per operation, paginated 50 workflows at a time, requires the Global bulk change permission, and includes only transitions common among the issues in a workflow that need no additional field updates, marking filtered results with `isTransitionsFiltered` (accessed 2026-09-27). These are documented ways to turn many per-candidate probes into one read.

Atlassian fact (what “mattering” can mean): Jira Cloud enforces three independent limits — a points quota (base 1 point per request plus per-object costs; the page says this regime applies to Forge, Connect and OAuth 2.0 3LO apps, while «API token-based traffic is not affected by this change, and will continue to be governed by existing burst rate limits»), per-tenant per-endpoint burst token buckets (default steady state 100 requests/second for GET, with endpoint-specific buckets such as the issue-read path at 150 rps), and per-issue write limits (20 writes per 2 seconds; 100 writes per 30 seconds). All return 429 with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-Reason`, and the same page’s optimization guidance says to «Cache stable responses: Use ETags and conditional headers to avoid re-fetching unchanged data», to keep bulk operations strategic, and to add jitter instead of relying on burst buffers (accessed 2026-09-27; page states last updated 21 Sep 2026).

Documentation check with an inference attached: the Jira Cloud REST API description for the issues endpoints (fetched 2026-09-27) documents no ETag, If-None-Match, Cache-Control or Last-Modified behaviour, and the Jira Cloud platform changelog text I fetched contains no entry announcing conditional-request support, while Atlassian’s generic advice names ETags. Inference (mine, to be tested rather than assumed): whether these responses actually carry validators, and whether a 304 costs fewer points or burst tokens, is an empirical question the experiment could settle by observing response headers and rate-limit headers before anything is designed around them.

Standards (framing for “the write changes the answer”): RFC 9111 §4.4 requires a cache to invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error status in response to an unsafe request method such as POST — the standard form of the claim-write invalidation the editor described — and RFC 9110 defines If-None-Match revalidation, where a matching validator yields 304 Not Modified (accessed 2026-09-27).

Practitioner guidance (criteria before building): AWS’s «Caching challenges and strategies» says a cache is considered when a dependency’s latency or throughput matters and its results can be reused across requests, notes that «cached data necessarily grows inconsistent with the source over time», recommends emitting metrics on cache hits and misses, total cache size and number of downstream requests, advises being «deliberate and empirical» about size, expiration and eviction, and requires resilience when the cache is unavailable; it also names the inline (cache management inside the data-access API) versus side-cache split. Fowler’s «Two Hard Things» page records the cache-invalidation folklore the design must respect (accessed 2026-09-27).

Patterns and existing solutions: Go’s `singleflight` is a «duplicate function call suppression mechanism» that shares one result among simultaneous callers, so it helps only when the repeated question is in flight at the same time; `lru-cache` for Node requires one of max/ttl/maxSize to bound storage and offers a `fetch` with `allowStaleOnFetchAbort` for stale-while-revalidate; OpenTelemetry’s JavaScript instrumentation documents counters for non-negative increasing values and histograms for distributions, using a `task.duration` histogram as its worked example — the vocabulary for reporting read counts and elapsed time (accessed 2026-09-27).

Project history lesson: the repository’s history contains a decided cache — HARN-49, Turborepo validation caching, Sep 2026 — that landed only with measured before/after transcripts, explicit declarations of what invalidates each cached task and stated limits; its first delivery was repaired because it cached work whose inputs it had not bounded. The legacy implementation and its record (docs/validation-caching.md and performance/) were later deleted in «Remove legacy implementation and retain Nexus rebuild design» (8935d55). Inference: in this project a cache idea is judged on declared dependencies and recorded measurement, not on the mechanism itself.

Classic principle worth naming: Amdahl’s law bounds the benefit of speeding up one part of a process by the share of time that part occupies, so even a perfect transitions cache could only move the fraction of the selection step attributable to those two reads (classic result; applying it to this idea is my inference, not a source claim).
options: Measure before adding state, in the author’s own framing: have the selection step report how often the same transitions question is asked within a run and how long the step takes. Because Jira’s answer is a function of issue, caller, status and query parameters, «the same question» is a precise tuple, and a measured reuse of zero inside one selection would itself be the evidence the experiment was for.

Name the governing principle before any cache exists (the editor’s question 3): «one selection works from one answer about a status» is a snapshot rule and tolerates the post-claim answer differing from the pre-claim one; «never ask the same question twice» is the rule RFC 9111 §4.4 formalises by invalidating on the write. The choice decides whether a hit at the claim boundary is even conceivable and what the cached thing promises.

Consider read composition as an alternative route to the same goal: fetch transitions alongside the issue (`expand=transitions`), alongside candidate reads, or through the bulk available-transitions endpoint. This removes reads without adding staleness, at documented costs (100-issue cap when bulkfetch expands transitions; Global bulk change permission and common-transition filtering for the bulk endpoint), with equality of the two answer shapes left for the experiment to check.

Consider provider-level revalidation only if the endpoint turns out to return validators: ETag/If-None-Match avoids re-transferring an unchanged answer but still spends a round trip, so it addresses quota and bandwidth rather than operator-visible latency, and its effect on points or burst tokens is not documented.

Distinguish caching an answer from coalescing in-flight work: if repeats come from overlapping attempts in one process, a single-flight style memo of the outstanding read is a smaller promise than a stored answer, and the project’s stated single-consumer queue assumption is what decides whether overlapping duplicates can occur at all.

Choose the currency (or currencies) the experiment judges — selection wall-clock, points quota, per-endpoint burst headroom, or operator-visible delay and failed selections — and state the threshold up front so the result reads either way; noting the Amdahl-style ceiling keeps the expected size of any win in view.

Keep the null result as a result: if the measured repeats are only the two different-status reads, the honest outcome is «no reuse inside a selection», the current snapshot design stands, and the recorded reading becomes evidence for later ideas — the HARN-49 record shows this project’s habit of keeping measurements and honest limits beside the decision.

If a cache is kept, decide deliberately where its guarantee lives: AWS’s inline-versus-side framing matches the project’s choice between the Jira adapter and the selection action, and the adapter contract’s «observed results» wording plus the AGENTS.md rule about keeping specialized guarantees with the component that needs them are the local considerations the idea can settle explicitly.

Nothing here argues against the experiment; it shows which readings would make the answer legible whichever way it turns out.","findings":["Project evidence (current read shape): on the fresh-claim path the idea selection calls the transitions endpoint twice — `transitionInto`/`selectFresh` read an issue’s permitted transitions to find the move into the active status, then `claim` reads them again right after the status write and stores the result as `transitions.fromActive` (src/task-engine/actions/select-idea/index.ts, around lines 155-201). The finite-delivery selection reads transitions once (src/task-engine/actions/select-task/index.ts, claim). So a retained or resumed selection that skips the pre-claim read does one read, not two.","Project evidence (why the second read exists): [publish-decision](src/task-engine/actions/publish-decision/index.ts) consumes the saved post-claim snapshot (`selection.transitions.fromActive`) rather than reading transitions again, and [docs/adapters/jira.md](docs/adapters/jira.md) states the run uses the selection snapshot for all agent work and publication and does not re-read the issue, comments or available transitions later. One of the two reads is already the design’s chosen substitute for a later read, so removing it changes a design promise rather than only a request count.","Project evidence (the two reads are different questions): Jira answers about the status in force when the read happens, and the claim write is what changes that status. Because the answer also depends on the caller’s permissions and workflow conditions, a status-aware cache cannot hit inside one fresh selection, and a cache that ignored status would serve the pre-move answer where the design wants the post-move one. This matches the editor’s reading; the experiment can confirm the scope empirically (per-candidate probes, retries, several selections per process).","Project evidence (current documented stance on caches): [docs/tech-stack.md](docs/tech-stack.md) says «Cache only deterministic validation results with their inputs declared. Live service operations and completion checks are never replaced by cached validation results.» A transitions read is a live provider observation rather than a validation result, so this idea sits beside that rule rather than clearly under it; as intent, that sentence is itself a current choice an idea may revise.","Project evidence (contracts bearing on where state would live): [docs/adapters/architecture.md](docs/adapters/architecture.md) says adapters «Return observed results», and AGENTS.md says to keep specialized guarantees within the component or action that needs them, with components depending on provider-owned public contracts. An adapter-level cache would need the adapter to own the invalidation guarantee, or “observed” quietly becomes “remembered”; an action-level cache keeps the staleness decision inside the selection it serves.","Project evidence (what the code can observe today): the transport the adapter accepts returns only `{status, body}` (src/adapters/jira.ts, JiraHttpResponse), so no timings and no response headers are visible to callers, and any non-2xx response — including 429 — becomes a fault with no retry loop. Counting and timing the reads therefore needs its own observation point, and today a rate-limit event surfaces as a failed selection rather than as a retry.","Project evidence (existing timing trail): activity-log entries are written with a receipt timestamp per activity packet (src/application/activity-log.ts) and the operator interface timestamps each entry once on receipt ([docs/operator-interface.md](docs/operator-interface.md)). The wall-clock span of a selection step is therefore partly recoverable from today’s logs, while individual Jira requests are not separately recorded.","Jira fact (transitions endpoint semantics): GET /rest/api/3/issue/{issueIdOrKey}/transitions «Returns either all transitions or a transition that can be performed by the user on an issue, based on the issue’s status»; a request for a transition that does not exist or cannot be performed returns an empty transitions list; the list is empty when the user lacks the Transition issues permission; the answer accepts `transitionId`, `includeUnavailableTransitions` (default false), `skipRemoteOnlyCondition` and `sortByOpsBarAndStatus`, and can be expanded with `transitions.fields` (Jira Cloud REST API v3, Issues; accessed 2026-09-27). The permission clause is why the same question can have different answers for different callers.","Jira fact (the same answer can be folded into other reads): GET /rest/api/3/issue/{issueIdOrKey} accepts `expand=transitions` («Returns all possible transitions for the issue»), and the Issue response schema carries a `transitions` array described as «The transitions that can be performed on the issue»; POST /rest/api/3/search/jql also accepts a transitions expand (accessed 2026-09-27). Whether the expanded list is identical to the dedicated endpoint’s answer — availability filtering, ordering, `isAvailable` flags — is something the experiment can compare directly for one issue and status.","Jira fact (bulk alternatives): POST /rest/api/3/issue/bulkfetch accepts a transitions expand but then caps at 100 issues per request (1,000 requires omitting it), and GET /rest/api/3/bulk/issues/transition returns available transitions for up to 1,000 issues per operation, paginated 50 workflows at a time, requires the Global bulk change permission, and includes only transitions common among the issues in a workflow that need no additional field updates, marking filtered results with `isTransitionsFiltered` (accessed 2026-09-27). These are documented ways to turn many per-candidate probes into one read.","Atlassian fact (what “mattering” can mean): Jira Cloud enforces three independent limits — a points quota (base 1 point per request plus per-object costs; the page says this regime applies to Forge, Connect and OAuth 2.0 3LO apps, while «API token-based traffic is not affected by this change, and will continue to be governed by existing burst rate limits»), per-tenant per-endpoint burst token buckets (default steady state 100 requests/second for GET, with endpoint-specific buckets such as the issue-read path at 150 rps), and per-issue write limits (20 writes per 2 seconds; 100 writes per 30 seconds). All return 429 with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-Reason`, and the same page’s optimization guidance says to «Cache stable responses: Use ETags and conditional headers to avoid re-fetching unchanged data», to keep bulk operations strategic, and to add jitter instead of relying on burst buffers (accessed 2026-09-27; page states last updated 21 Sep 2026).","Documentation check with an inference attached: the Jira Cloud REST API description for the issues endpoints (fetched 2026-09-27) documents no ETag, If-None-Match, Cache-Control or Last-Modified behaviour, and the Jira Cloud platform changelog text I fetched contains no entry announcing conditional-request support, while Atlassian’s generic advice names ETags. Inference (mine, to be tested rather than assumed): whether these responses actually carry validators, and whether a 304 costs fewer points or burst tokens, is an empirical question the experiment could settle by observing response headers and rate-limit headers before anything is designed around them.","Standards (framing for “the write changes the answer”): RFC 9111 §4.4 requires a cache to invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error status in response to an unsafe request method such as POST — the standard form of the claim-write invalidation the editor described — and RFC 9110 defines If-None-Match revalidation, where a matching validator yields 304 Not Modified (accessed 2026-09-27).","Practitioner guidance (criteria before building): AWS’s «Caching challenges and strategies» says a cache is considered when a dependency’s latency or throughput matters and its results can be reused across requests, notes that «cached data necessarily grows inconsistent with the source over time», recommends emitting metrics on cache hits and misses, total cache size and number of downstream requests, advises being «deliberate and empirical» about size, expiration and eviction, and requires resilience when the cache is unavailable; it also names the inline (cache management inside the data-access API) versus side-cache split. The legacy implementation and its record (docs/validation-caching.md and performance/) were later deleted in «Remove legacy implementation and retain Nexus rebuild design» (8935d55). Inference: in this project a cache idea is judged on declared dependencies and recorded measurement, not on the mechanism itself.","Classic principle worth naming: Amdahl’s law bounds the benefit of speeding up one part of a process by the share of time that part occupies, so even a perfect transitions cache could only move the fraction of the selection step attributable to those two reads (classic result; applying it to this idea is my inference, not a source claim)."],"options":["Measure before adding state, in the author’s own framing: have the selection step report how often the same transitions question is asked within a run and how long the step takes. Because Jira’s answer is a function of issue, caller, status and query parameters, «the same question» is a precise tuple, and a measured reuse of zero inside one selection would itself be the evidence the experiment was for.","Name the governing principle before any cache exists (the editor’s question 3): «one selection works from one answer about a status» is a snapshot rule and tolerates the post-claim answer differing from the pre-claim one; «never ask the same question twice» is the rule RFC 9111 §4.4 formalises by invalidating on the write. The choice decides whether a hit at the claim boundary is even conceivable and what the cached thing promises.","Consider read composition as an alternative route to the same goal: fetch transitions alongside the issue (`expand=transitions`), alongside candidate reads, or through the bulk available-transitions endpoint. This removes reads without adding staleness, at documented costs (100-issue cap when bulkfetch expands transitions; Global bulk change permission and common-transition filtering for the bulk endpoint), with equality of the two answer shapes left for the experiment to check.","Consider provider-level revalidation only if the endpoint turns out to return validators: ETag/If-None-Match avoids re-transferring an unchanged answer but still spends a round trip, so it addresses quota and bandwidth rather than operator-visible latency, and its effect on points or burst tokens is not documented.","Distinguish caching an answer from coalescing in-flight work: if repeats come from overlapping attempts in one process, a single-flight style memo of the outstanding read is a smaller promise than a stored answer, and the project’s stated single-consumer queue assumption is what decides whether overlapping duplicates can occur at all.","Choose the currency (or currencies) the experiment judges — selection wall-clock, points quota, per-endpoint burst headroom, or operator-visible delay and failed selections — and state the threshold up front so the result reads either way; noting the Amdahl-style ceiling keeps the expected size of any win in view.","Keep the null result as a result: if the measured repeats are only the two different-status reads, the honest outcome is «no reuse inside a selection», the current snapshot design stands, and the recorded reading becomes evidence for later ideas — the HARN-49 record shows this project’s habit of keeping measurements and honest limits beside the decision.","If a cache is kept, decide deliberately where its guarantee lives: AWS’s inline-versus-side framing matches the project’s choice between the Jira adapter and the selection action, and the adapter contract’s «observed results» wording plus the AGENTS.md rule about keeping specialized guarantees with the component that needs them are the local considerations the idea can settle explicitly."],"sources":[{"title":"Jira Cloud platform — Rate limiting (points quota, burst buckets, per-issue write limits, caching guidance)","link":"https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/jira/platform/rate-limiting/","accessed":"2026-09-27"},{"title":"Jira Cloud REST API v3 — Issues (Get issue with expand=transitions; output.response: The proposal keeps its shape: count and time the Jira transition reads one idea selection makes, then judge from what shows up whether a cache earns its state — and let 'no material repeats' be a real result. The editor's nuance holds up in the code: on a fresh claim the two reads are answers about different statuses (pre-claim lookup for the move out of Submitted, then the post-claim snapshot publication consumes), and the claim write is exactly the invalidation point, so a cache surviving it would serve the pre-move answer where the design wants the fresh one. That leaves retries, per-candidate probes or repeated selections as candidates for genuine reuse, and measurement can settle which — so I left the author's words open rather than narrowing them. Three questions would usefully develop it: which reads are in scope, which currency (wall-clock, quota, burst headroom, operator-visible delay) decides that reads matter, and — only if a cache is kept — whether the principle is one snapshot per selection or never ask the same question twice, and where that state lives. Two research notes: transitions can often be folded into an existing read (expand=transitions) or a bulk available-transitions call with no cached state, and validator/ETag behaviour is unverified, so it stays an experiment too. Correct me if 'repeated reads' meant something narrower.
output.reason: Author's experiment preserved as an exploration; refinement adds measurement before cache state, keeps the null result first-class, and surfaces the scope, currency and governing-principle questions.

refinedIdea.idea: Explore caching the Jira transitions one idea selection reads: count and time those reads first, to learn whether repeats are material and whether a cache earns its state. The principle is evidence before optimization; the author expects the complexity may not pay off, and an honestly measured null result ends the exploration.
refinedIdea.projectFit: Fits the project's evidence-first direction: AGENTS.md requires evidence of a bottleneck before performance complexity, and the idea-refinement spec explicitly allows exploring a performance idea before measurement. The probe is cheap today — the Jira adapter takes an injectable transport, and the test helper records every operation call.
refinedIdea.feasibility: Instrument the selection's reads to attribute requests to distinct questions and attempts; activity-log timestamps give a partial wall-clock trail. Because one fresh selection's two reads answer different statuses and the claim write invalidates the first, measurement should reveal which same-question repeats actually exist, and documented composition options (transitions expand, bulk endpoint) remove reads without cached state.
openQuestions: Which reads actually repeat — pre-claim lookup, post-claim snapshot, per-candidate probes, retries, or repeat selections — and often enough to matter?
Which currency judges 'material': selection wall-clock, quota or burst headroom, or operator-visible delay and failed selections?
If a cache is kept, does one-snapshot-per-selection or never-ask-twice govern it, and where would its state live?

Named read-composition alternatives (expand=transitions, bulk available-transitions) and left scope, judgement currency and the governing principle as open questions.

output.assessment: Pursuing revision 1 is justified as a small evidence-first experiment, and the editor's response handles the one factual hazard that could have made it incoherent. I verified the read shape in the code: a fresh selection reads transitions pre-claim for the move into the active status and again post-claim to snapshot what publication later consumes, so a cache keyed on the question saves nothing there, and the claim write is indeed the invalidation point — the editor's reading is correct, and I withdraw any concern that the repeated pre/post-claim reads are a cacheable target. That does not narrow the experiment: counting first settles which repeats exist (per-candidate probes, retries, repeat selections), so scope is decided by evidence rather than guesswork. Feasibility is real and cheap: the scripted Jira adapter already records every operation call, so per-selection request counts are observable without new runtime state, and activity-log timestamps give a partial duration trail. Complexity is bounded because no cache is committed; the null result is explicitly a success and matches the project's evidence-before-optimization rule. Remaining uncertainty about which currency judges "mattering" and where cached state would live are carried as open questions in the revision, not obstacles to pursuing.
suggestions: Produce the first evidence where it is already cheap: per-selection request counts from a recording test double answer whether same-question repeats exist at all, with no runtime instrumentation and no cache. State plainly which currency the probe can yield this way, and treat real Jira latency or rate-limit headroom as requiring an explicit timing observation point later, so a "no evidence either way" outcome is avoided.

If measured repeats turn out to live only in retry/recovery paths or per-candidate probing, weigh the research's read-composition options (transitions folded into an existing issue read, or the bulk available-transitions call) against cached state before designing invalidation; they remove reads without staleness, which fits the project's simplicity rules.
